analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue brand-name companies that refuse to sell them samples for testing.
analysis.headline: With 68 cosponsors from both parties and two unanimous committee approvals, the bill was placed on the House calendar and never received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Some brand-name drug companies use safety programs called REMS to refuse selling samples of their drugs to generic and biosimilar makers, who need those samples to prove their cheaper copies are equivalent. This bill would let those copycat makers sue a brand company that refuses to sell samples on fair terms, with a court able to force the sale, award attorney fees, and add a penalty tied to the brand company's revenue during the delay. It would also let generic makers use alternative but equally safe safety controls instead of being forced into the brand company's program.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay brand-name prices because a cheaper generic or biosimilar is delayed. When a brand company stonewalls a generic maker's testing, the lower-cost version stays off the market and the brand keeps charging monopoly prices. The bill shortens that delay by giving generic makers a fast, enforceable way to get the samples they need.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: A generic or biosimilar developer who asks to buy sufficient samples of an approved drug and is refused within a 31-day deadline can sue the brand license holder in federal court [S5].

A court that finds the brand company refused without a legitimate business justification can order the sale, award the generic maker attorney fees and costs, and impose a monetary penalty large enough to deter the conduct, capped at the brand's revenue on that drug during the delay [S5].

The bill lets FDA-authorized generic developers use safety protections comparable to the brand's safety program (REMS) rather than being forced into a single shared system, removing another lever for delay [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers lose the ability to slow generic competition by withholding samples or controlling the safety program, which cuts into monopoly profits on those drugs. The bill also shields brand companies from liability for mishandling by the generic developer and lets courts order sales quickly, which brand companies argued exposes them to litigation they cannot fully control.

drawbacks.text: Brand companies and their trade group argued the bill invites lawsuits over business judgment and exposes them to penalties and forced sales on terms a court, not the manufacturer, defines [S5].

Allowing generic developers to obtain a safety-restricted drug outside the brand's safety program raises safety concerns; the bill addresses this by requiring the Health and Human Services Secretary to authorize such access and impose comparable safeguards [S5].

The deterrence penalty is capped at the brand company's revenue during the delay period, which some fair-minded critics on both sides considered either too weak to deter or too broad a punishment for a judgment call.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and immediate: faster generic competition on drugs where the main obstacle is a brand company's refusal to sell samples, which means lower prices for patients and payers. The main costs fall on brand manufacturers, and the safety risk is mitigated by requiring an FDA-type authorization with comparable safeguards. The bill is not perfectly designed — the penalty cap and litigation exposure were legitimately contested — but the mechanism is narrow and targeted rather than a broad new liability regime.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared both House committees unanimously and was placed on the House calendar in May 2019, but no one ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 5, 2019 by Rep. Cicilline with original cosponsors including Reps. Sensenbrenner, Nadler, Collins of Georgia, Welch, and McKinley [S1].
The Energy and Commerce subcommittee forwarded it to the full committee amended by voice vote on March 27, 2019 [S7].
On April 3, 2019 the committee ordered the bill reported amended by a vote of 50-0 [S7].
Both the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees reported the bill on May 10, 2019, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 33 [S5], [S7].
The last recorded action is the Judiciary Committee's supplemental report filed May 16, 2019; the bill never received a House floor vote [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: because no vote was ever taken, they kept the ability to control access to drug samples and safety programs that can delay cheaper generic and biosimilar competition. Patients waiting for those cheaper versions continued paying brand-name prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and their profits

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor joined by senior Republicans — with 55 of 231 House Democrats and 13 of 197 House Republicans cosponsoring, and the committee vote was 50-0.

industries.note: The bill strips away a tool these companies use to keep cheaper competitors off the market: refusing to sell samples of a safety-restricted drug, or forcing the generic into the brand's own safety program. Their interest in keeping that tool runs directly against patients' interest in lower prices.

The bill gives these companies a legal right to buy the samples they need to develop lower-cost versions of brand-name drugs, on court-enforceable terms. Their gain — faster market entry — is the same outcome patients want.
